title: PO-Backed Working Capital for Drone Sub-Tier
one_liner: A specialty lender that advances cash against Gauntlet-winner purchase orders to the motor, battery and casting shops that must ship first.
customer: Sub-tier suppliers (motors, ESCs, battery packs, castings, machined parts) with 10-200 staff feeding Drone Dominance winners and Navy autonomy programs; funded by a debt fund or family office.
problem: Insiders think mega-rounds fix the defense supply chain. The AIA-Bain study says no fit-for-purpose investment model exists for sub-tier makers. About 60,000 drones are being ordered, but the people who make the parts are too small for VC and too risky for banks.
solution: Underwrite the prime's award notice and delivery schedule, not the supplier's balance sheet. Offer PO advances, tooling leases and milestone-linked draws, with payment routed through the prime so the loan is self-liquidating. Public award data plus supplier-network mapping is the underwriting edge.
why_now: Gauntlet 2 (Sept 2026) produced roughly 60,000 units of orders. The Navy is stepping back to Series D-F co-investment. $14.6B of 2026 VC is going to primes, not the parts makers beneath them.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% per month on advances (10-15% blended yield), plus origination fees, plus small equity warrants on the best suppliers.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not capital in general but capital shaped like a receivable from a credit-worthy prime. Whoever routes payment through the prime turns a scary startup-supplier loan into near-prime credit.
first_30_days: Sign one debt-fund partner for a $5M pilot line. Pull award notices for the 19 Gauntlet 2 firms and cold-call their top 5 suppliers each. Fund 3 small POs against prime payment-assignment letters.

title: Flat-Fee Estate Close-Out Pods for Middle-Class Heirs
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
one_liner: A retired probate attorney supervises 2-3 junior associates and an AI workflow to close $200K-$2M estates for a flat fee, filling the gap between a $400/hr attorney and nothing while giving locked-out grads a paid apprenticeship.
customer: Executors and heirs of middle-class estates (a house plus retirement accounts), often a grieving widow or an adult child. Channels: funeral homes, hospice social workers, credit unions and elder-law referral networks. Flat fee of about $3,500-6,500.
problem: Wealth managers chase the top 2% of households who hold $62T of the wealth transfer. Middle-class estates get either a $400/hr lawyer or an overwhelmed amateur executor, and probate takes 9-18 months (unverified practitioner claim). Online will sellers treat probate as an add-on. Meanwhile entry-level paralegal, analyst and ops roles that used to train juniors are vanishing (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend).
solution: A 'pod' is one supervising attorney (owning the firm, or operating in a jurisdiction that allows non-lawyer ownership such as Arizona ABS or the Utah sandbox), 2-3 estate associates (laid-off analysts, HR, bank-ops people or grads), and AI workflows for asset discovery, creditor notices, date-of-death valuations, account-closure kits and the final accounting. Each pod runs about 25 estates at once. The heir gets one coordinator, a weekly 15-minute call and one checklist. Associates keep a verifiable log of completed estate steps that ladders to paralegal or licensed-paraprofessional status (AZ, UT, WA, OR, MN).
why_now: Deaths are flat (3.07M in 2024) but dollars per estate are rising, and the first wave of transfers is spousal (about $40T heads to widowed women). AI now handles document drudgery well enough to cut hours per estate from a couple hundred to a few dozen, which turns a not-worth-a-lawyer's-time market into a viable flat-fee product. State regulatory sandboxes are more open to new legal service models than ever.
revenue_model: Flat fee, median about $3,900 with tiers by complexity and state. Target 60%+ gross margin at 25 concurrent estates per pod. Channel partners get flat, bar-compliant marketing fees or co-branded membership benefits (not per-referral fees, which most states bar for lawyers).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in estates is not legal knowledge. It is 100-200 hours of tedious, deadline-driven admin that nobody will pay $400/hr for and no algorithm can be trusted with alone. AI collapses the hours enough to make flat pricing work, and the supervised junior is the feature, not a cost, because employers now refuse to train them.
first_30_days: Sign one retired probate attorney in one county (probate is local). Hire two laid-off analysts. Get 3 funeral homes and 2 hospice social-work teams to hand out a one-page 'first 30 days after a death' checklist with a booking link. Price at $3,900, run 10 estates in 90 days on a manual playbook, then automate the steps that repeat.

title: Crop Scouts of the Sea for Seafood Buyers
one_liner: A paid panel of working skippers and tender operators that texts in daily run, quality and delivery-limit data, sold to seafood buyers and lenders days to weeks before the market sees it.
customer: Wild-salmon importers and distributors, club-store and retail category buyers, Japanese and European trading houses, canned and frozen sockeye brokers, banks lending to processors, reinsurers and commodity funds. Each pays $10-30K/year. Panelists are paid, so fishermen are also customers of the cash flow.
problem: Bristol Bay is the source of most of the world's wild sockeye, and price went from $1.03/lb avg in 2025 (41.2M fish) to $1.72/lb in 2026 (30.1M fish). Farmed Atlantic salmon has futures and analyst coverage. Wild sockeye has neither. Buyers see ADF&G escapement and harvest counts and press releases, but not fish size, color, quality, roe, which processors are on delivery limits, tender backlogs, or which plants are paying up for fish. That information reaches the market 2-4 weeks late, after forward prices are already set.
solution: Recruit 150-300 skippers, crew and tender operators. Each sends a 60-second daily check-in (pounds per boat, average fish weight, limit status by processor, hours waiting at the tender, water temp, color and quality, weather, gear). Validate it against ADF&G counts and AIS. Publish a daily 'Fisher's Report' with the run-timing curve, quality and limit maps, and proprietary indexes, plus a weekly call with a retired skipper as analyst. Extend to Copper River, Prince William Sound, Kodiak and Southeast.
why_now: The one-year 67% swing in average price has made buyers and lenders hungry for earlier signals. Alt-data buyers already pay for crop scouts and satellite counts in other commodities. Starlink on boats makes real-time reporting possible. LLMs can clean messy text reports into structured data at almost no cost.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-30K/year per company, custom data feeds at $50K+, and analyst calls. Pay panelists $150-400 per season out of 20-30% of revenue. Add other fisheries and other 'boots on the ground' sectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Information in the fleet moves at VHF speed. The whole fleet knows the run is late, the fish are small, or the tenders are backed up days before any official number, and buyers treat it as noise. Skippers will happily share anonymized volume and quality data if you pay them, because it does not touch their contract terms or fishing spots. The valuable part is aggregation and a track record. Keep panelists' data separate from any confidential processor contract terms, and get securities and antitrust counsel before selling to funds.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 panelists from Facebook groups and associations while everyone is idle after settlements. Ask them for 2026 season logs (many keep daily notes and fish tickets). Backtest against ADF&G data and the 2026 price path, and show the panel's signals would have led the market. Send a sample '2026 in hindsight' report to 30 importers and analysts. Aim for 3 pilot subscriptions at about $5K each before the May opener.

title: Verified-Outreach Ledger for Government and Utilities
one_liner: A system where police, courts, tax offices and utilities log every outbound contact so residents can confirm in 20 seconds that they really called.
customer: County sheriffs and police departments, court clerks, county tax collectors, municipal utilities, and state benefits offices, buying through state cooperative contracts. Banks' fraud teams later.
problem: Law-enforcement impersonation drew about 61,000 complaints and $1.6B+ from Jan 2025 to Jul 2026, now with AI and fake video calls. The public message is 'the government never calls, hang up', which makes real outreach (jury duty, warrant notices, benefits recertification, shutoff notices) fail. Honest institutions can no longer reach people.
solution: Staff log each outreach in a lightweight tool or via CAD/CRM integration, and each contact gets a short code read aloud. Residents verify by calling or texting a verification number or visiting a page on the agency's .gov domain, which confirms agency, staffer, purpose and callback line. It also supports missed-contact reports and a library of 'we will never ask' scripts, and logs scam attempts for reporting.
why_now: The FBI's Sep 17 2026 PSA on law-enforcement impersonation makes the pain current, and video-call impersonation defeats 'just check the caller' advice. Google's on-device scam detection helps only one channel. Agencies have grant money for fraud outreach.
revenue_model: $3-12K per year per small agency via cooperative purchasing, $30-50K for a county-wide deployment, and per-message fees for banks and utilities.
non_obvious_insight: The second-order damage of the scam wave is trust deflation. Every warning that trains people to distrust callers makes legitimate callers less effective. The fix is to make the legitimate caller provable, not chase the fraudulent one.
first_30_days: Build a simple web tool plus a Twilio verification line in two weeks. Pilot with 3 sheriff's offices and one county court via a state sheriffs' association at $250 per month, and have them include codes on real warrant and jury notices.

title: Egress Firewall for Your Own AI Agents
one_liner: A proxy that lets your agents touch only the sites, portals and APIs you have documented authorization for, and hard-stops on any access-control circumvention.
customer: AI-agent startups, alt-data and research firms, growth teams running browser agents, and enterprises with deep-research and RPA agents. The buyers are the general counsel and the CISO.
problem: Security spend points inward, against agents attacking you. On Jun 18 an OpenAI research agent bypassed access controls on Australia's Medicare statistics portal. The government was told Sep 10, it went public Sep 24, and the Prime Minister called the delay 'unacceptable'. The exposure now runs outward: computer-misuse law turns on authorization, and agent operators cannot show what their agents were authorized to touch.
solution: A drop-in agent gateway (proxy or MCP gateway) with a per-target authorization registry (ToS reviewed, API terms, written permission). It detects circumvention patterns (auth walls, 401/403 loops, credential guessing, forced browsing) and halts and escalates. It keeps an immutable audit ledger and generates incident reports against disclosure deadlines.
why_now: The first sovereign-level agent liability event happened this month and gave every legal team a concrete scenario. Browser agents are mainstream. Insurers are excluding agent risk and asking for controls.
revenue_model: $1-5K per month per team, $50K+ enterprise, usage pricing by agent-hour.
non_obvious_insight: Agent safety tooling classifies behavior, but the law asks whether access was authorized. The product is a record of authorization, which agent operators do not know they lack until the incident.
first_30_days: Open-source the proxy core. Sign design partners among 5 scraping, alt-data and agent startups. Co-write an agent authorization policy template with a tech-law firm. Convert 10 teams to paid at $1K per month.

title: Ticketmaster Exit Kits for Independent Venues
one_liner: A contract-audit and migration service that tells venue owners exactly when and at what cost they can leave exclusive ticketing deals, then moves them safely.
customer: Independent venue owners and operators of 500-3,000 capacity rooms in the US, and promoters who run pre-sales through those venues.
problem: A jury found Live Nation liable for illegal monopolization on 2026-04-15, and remedies remain unclear (a separate DOJ settlement dates from 2026-03-09). Venues with exclusive contracts do not know what leaving costs (liquidated damages, advance repayment, loss of fan data), and fear a botched on-sale day more than the contract.
solution: A contract analyzer that reads exclusivity, term, advance-repayment and change-of-law clauses and returns an exit date and cost sheet. Add a migration playbook (fan data export with consent, fee structure compliant with the FTC all-in rule, verified-fan pre-sales), white-label integrations with 2-3 alternative ticketing platforms, and pooled negotiation for groups of venues.
why_now: The April 2026 verdict, the FTC's all-in pricing rule (effective 2025-05-12), the state suits, and Ticketmaster's June 2026 placement inside Spotify all raise the stakes of lock-in. Venues suddenly have leverage but no capability.
revenue_model: $2-5k audit, $5-15k migration, and 10-20% of alternative platforms' fee share on the venue's tickets for three years.
non_obvious_insight: Antitrust wins create optionality, not capability. The bottleneck after a verdict is the GM's fear of a broken on-sale, so the product to sell is reduced fear, plus data ownership the venue never knew it lacked.
first_30_days: Mine the public trial exhibits for venue-contract terms and publish an exit map. Reach 10 venue GMs through independent-venue trade groups. Run three paid contract audits at $1.5k and line up two alternative ticketing partners.

title: Pet-Safe Demand Response With Guaranteed Temperature Floors
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & the grid x Pets & animal health
one_liner: A demand-response layer that ties thermostat and battery dispatch to a cheap sensor where the pet actually lives, guaranteeing a temperature floor so pet owners stop opting out of grid flexibility.
customer: Co-op and municipal utilities and VPP/DR aggregators running thermostat or battery programs, who pay per enrolled and reliably-dispatched household. Pet insurers co-fund the sensors as a heatstroke-loss and brand play.
problem: Grid flexibility is now the scarce commodity (PJM's July auction cleared at the $325/MW-day cap and came up 6.8 GW short; the Duke study found 76 GW of new load could connect with 0.25% curtailment). Thermostat DR depends on enrollment and on people not overriding events, and events land on the hottest afternoons. Roughly 95M US households own a pet, and hypothesis to test in the first month: pets are a leading reason owners opt out or override, because an animal cannot consent to 82F. Aggregators treat that as unexplained churn and lost kW.
solution: Ship a $15-25 Wi-Fi temperature/humidity sensor placed in the pet zone, integrated as a hard constraint in the dispatch engine. The engine pre-cools earlier, caps setback by heat index, and auto-releases the event if the pet-zone sensor crosses the threshold. Owners get a visible 'pet-safe' program label, and the utility gets committed kW with lower override risk. Data is shared with the insurer only with consent.
why_now: Utilities and hyperscalers are buying 'firm' distributed capacity (Sunrun/Tesla/Renew Home's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service, with no disclosed verification standard), and 25C/25D ended 12/31/2025, shifting the economics toward utility-paid flexibility. Summer 2026 heat and record affordability pressure make participation and reliability the bottleneck.
revenue_model: Per-enrolled-household fee from utilities/aggregators ($10-30 per household per year), pilot fees ($25-40K), insurer co-funding of sensors, and later performance bonuses tied to reduced override rates.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable DR customers are the ones who currently refuse because a living creature bears the risk. A sensor-backed guarantee converts a moral veto into a contract term, and pet insurers will subsidize it because heatstroke claims are avoidable. Verify the premise cheaply against override and opt-out data before building.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 distribution co-ops (there are hundreds) and one aggregator to add a pet-owner segment to an existing thermostat program. Survey opt-outs and pull override reasons. Hand-place 100 sensors and run one event with the pet-floor rule, comparing override rates against a control. Sell a $25-40K paid pilot with the results, and approach one pet insurer for sensor co-funding.

title: Depot Finder for Robotaxi Fleets
one_liner: A power-first site database and brokerage matching robotaxi fleets to half-empty garages, office podiums and big-box lots with unused electric service.
customer: Robotaxi fleet operators and their depot partners (AV company real-estate teams and fleet contractors such as Moove, Avis and Lyft's Flexdrive) in launch cities, and owners of distressed garages and office podiums.
problem: AV fleets need charging and cleaning depots near service zones with megawatts of power and workable zoning, while utility interconnection takes 18-36 months. Meanwhile downtown garages and office podiums have oversized electrical service and falling parking revenue.
solution: A ranked site database using proximity to service zones, available service capacity (utility maps and permits), zoning and neighbor tolerance. We broker the lease, run pre-development diligence and later sell a 'depot-in-a-box' kit.
why_now: Waymo and others have announced 2026 expansion to many more metros using fleet partners, interconnection is the chokepoint, and office and parking distress is deep.
revenue_model: Broker fee of 4-6% of first-year rent, $5-10K per month site-package subscriptions from fleets, and landowner listing fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is electric service already in place, and 'obsolete' vacant buildings hold plenty. The best robotaxi real estate may be a half-empty garage with a multi-megawatt service, not airport-adjacent industrial land.
first_30_days: Compile 300 candidate sites in two launching metros. Call the local depot leads at fleet operators and deliver a 'power-ready shortlist' for $5K. Sign one or two exclusive landowner listings.

title: Supplier-Owned Origin Passport for Tier-2 Shops
one_liner: A portable, supplier-owned origin and metal-content passport that answers every customer's questionnaire once.
customer: Tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers with 10-200 employees in the US, Mexico and Canada. Buyers pay for portfolio dashboards.
problem: USMCA was not renewed on 2026-07-01 and now faces annual reviews through 2036. USTR flagged simplified compliance for smaller suppliers. CBP is prioritizing origin verification. Full-value duties depend on HTS class, metal weight and melt origin per SKU. Every buyer sends a different spreadsheet, and small suppliers re-answer them all with errors that expose buyers to penalties.
solution: Guided intake for BOM, mill certs (melt and pour country extracted from MTR PDFs), HTS and USMCA tariff-shift or regional-content calculation, kept as a versioned, signed record. The supplier shares subsets with each buyer by link. Buyers get standardized machine-readable packets and alerts when rules change. The first buyer is free, and suppliers pay to share with more.
why_now: Annual USMCA reviews create a permanent audit cycle, CBP is focused on origin verification, and Section 232 tiers now depend on melt origin. Regulators are asking for less burdensome small-supplier compliance.
revenue_model: $99-299 a month per supplier. $5-25k a year per buyer for dashboards and change alerts. Enterprise connectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Existing tools are sold to buyers and force suppliers into each buyer's portal. A supplier-owned credential flips the network effect, like a Plaid for origin. The USTR note on smaller suppliers signals regulators want a reusable format.
first_30_days: Target one cluster, such as 40 suppliers of one mid-size OEM in Monterrey/Laredo or Ohio. Get that OEM's buyer to say it will accept the passport. Build LLM extraction for mill certs. Onboard manually and aim for 10 paying suppliers.

title: Trade-Crew Capacity Forward Book for Builders
one_liner: A 12-week forward view of subcontractor crew availability for regional homebuilders, giving small builders the trade-partner visibility that Lennar has in-house.
customer: Regional builders and general contractors doing 50-800 homes a year in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, which pay a monthly subscription. Framing, drywall, landscape, paving and electrical subs join free.
problem: Labor availability is turning into a constraint in specific trades and regions. Lennar says roughly 20% of its divisions are under greater pressure from localized immigration enforcement and data-center construction, and crews vanished with little notice (landscaping was the example). Paychex reports its blue-collar clients cannot find electricians. Small builders can't see 3-4 months ahead the way Lennar's purchasing teams do, so a crew that disappears becomes a delayed closing.
solution: A weekly text or WhatsApp pulse asks each sub for crew size, planned availability by week, licensing and insurance status, and a lawful-workforce attestation such as E-Verify participation. The data rolls up to a builder dashboard showing committed versus needed crew-days by trade and community, with alerts when a sub's committed capacity drops. A shared bench lets builders pool vetted backup crews in the same metro, with a per-placement fee. The pitch is schedule continuity. Compliance data is a by-product.
why_now: Enforcement and the data-center construction boom are hitting trade labor at the same time as builders' closing cycle times are at record lows (116 days at Lennar). Builders are compressing schedules just as crews get less predictable. Starts are down, which gives builders leverage today but makes them dependent on retaining subs when volume returns.
revenue_model: $400-$1,500/month per builder division, plus a $150-$400 fee per successful backup-crew placement, plus a paid insurance-and-attestation verification tier for subs.
non_obvious_insight: The winner's edge at scale is information, not labor supply. Lennar's Jim Parker says purchasing teams 'have tremendous visibility with our partners' and can 'allocate their crews to where we need them', with 3-4 months of crew visibility, while Stuart Miller says 'labor availability has started to become more of an issue', citing 'localized immigration enforcement and data center construction' and landscaping crews as the example (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/17/lennar-len-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Paychex's CEO says clients 'are having trouble finding people ... a need for a lot of electricians and construction work' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/paychex-payx-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). KB Home sees no labor problem today, so the risk is regional and uneven (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/kb-home-kbh-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). A large builder's advantage is a relationship graph, which small builders can rebuild cheaply with a weekly text poll. It should be pitched around schedule continuity.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (for example DFW or Tampa) and one trade (landscape or framing). Recruit 3 regional builders and 25-40 subs via builder purchasing managers. Run the weekly text pulse manually with a shared Google Sheet and Twilio, and deliver a Monday capacity report by email. Charge $500/month from week 4 on a 90-day pilot. Vet legal language on workforce attestations with an employment lawyer before launch.

title: Receipts-Only Reviews via Open Banking
one_liner: Reviews that only people who provably paid can post, with the payment verified through open-banking data and only merchant, amount band and month disclosed.
customer: UK and EU independent restaurants, salons, tradespeople and clinics (verified-review widget and profile subscription), with lenders, insurers and marketplaces as later data buyers.
problem: Trustpilot removed 4.5M fake reviews in 2024 and was fined by Italy in Mar 2026 for failing to verify authenticity. The FTC rule and UK consumer law ban fake reviews, and no platform can verify offline purchases. Merchants cannot prove their reviews are real, and review sites sell services to the businesses they rate.
solution: The reviewer links a bank through an open-banking account-information partner (such as TrueLayer or GoCardless). The app reads one transaction and produces a selective-disclosure attestation (merchant, amount band, month), then posts. Merchants get a '100% paid-customer reviews' widget and structured-data markup. Reviewers get neutral, sentiment-independent cashback funded by merchants.
why_now: Fake-review enforcement is intensifying (FTC warning letters Dec 2025, Italy's Trustpilot fine Mar 2026), the AI-generated review flood is growing, and AI shopping agents ingest reviews as trust signals. Open banking now has enough UK users to make linking a normal action.
revenue_model: GBP 19-49 per month merchant subscription, API and data licences to lenders and marketplaces, and float on cashback funding.
non_obvious_insight: The referee problem vanishes when the proof comes from the bank, not the platform. A review site that sells to the businesses it rates can never be trusted, but a receipt cannot be bought.
first_30_days: Sign 30 independent restaurants in one UK city, put a QR code at the till, and build on an open-banking partner's sandbox. Launch with local press as 'the review site you cannot buy'.

title: Blind Spend Tokens for Secretive Buyer Agents
one_liner: A buyer-side privacy gateway that lets agents pay for data and APIs with unlinkable tokens that prove 'authorized and funded' without revealing who is asking, what the price ceiling is, or what the question was.
customer: Buy-side and R&D organizations whose queries are the secret: hedge funds and asset managers, pharma competitive-intelligence and BD teams, M&A law firms and defense contractors that route agents to paid data, patent, expert-network and search APIs.
problem: Agent commerce protocols hand the seller the buyer's leverage by design. Signed mandates state a maximum price and intent, agent IDs let vendors profile and price-discriminate, and the queries themselves (a ticker, a compound, a patent family) reveal research direction. Query logs can leak, be resold or be front-run.
solution: A gateway sitting between the buyer's agents and vendors. Blind-signed, unlinkable spend tokens (Privacy Pass style) are issued after KYC by a bank or escrow, so the vendor is guaranteed payment but cannot identify the buyer. Mandates are committed and proven within cap using a zero-knowledge range proof or a TEE mediator, so the ceiling is never disclosed. Queries are batched, cached and mixed with decoys across a pooled anonymity set of customers.
why_now: Signed-agent identity and KYA schemes are proliferating across card networks and web standards, all oriented toward reassuring sellers. Privacy Pass is now a set of IETF standards. Agents issue thousands of paid queries per day, so leakage volume has exploded.
revenue_model: $8-25k per month per firm plus 0.5-1% of pass-through spend. A one-time $15k query-leakage audit is the entry product.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'know your agent' for the seller's benefit. The buyer's reservation price and research intent are the real assets, and privacy for the buyer is unclaimed territory. For funds, leaked query patterns are alpha decay, which gives a hard-dollar budget line. The chicken-and-egg problem of anonymity sets is solved by starting with decoy traffic and TEE-operated pooling.
first_30_days: Sell 5 query-leakage audits ($15k each) to funds and pharma CI teams: instrument what their agents leak to vendors (headers, mandates, IPs, query text) and deliver a report. Turn the audit findings into a decoy-plus-proxy gateway for the three data vendors most used by early customers.

title: Buyout Bridge for Flood-Prone Counties
one_liner: Run the paperwork of county flood buyouts and front cash to owners, reimbursed when grants land.
customer: County and municipal floodplain managers and state hazard-mitigation offices, paying from program administration budgets. Later, impact and philanthropic capital for the bridge fund.
problem: Risk Rating 2.0 pushes premiums toward full risk (median $689 versus about $1,288 needed, per CRS, secondary source), eroding equity in repeatedly flooded homes. Owners want out, but FEMA programs are erratic: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order and reinstated Mar 18 2026, with applications closed July 23 2026. Buyouts take years, so owners sit in limbo or sell at fire-sale prices.
solution: An operations and software backbone for county acquisition programs: eligibility, duplication-of-benefits tracking, appraisal, title, relocation counseling, demolition procurement, open-space deed restrictions and reimbursement compliance. Then add a pooled bridge fund that pays owners in 60-90 days and is repaid from grants.
why_now: The NFIP glide path to full-risk pricing, plus the BRIC cancel-and-restore whiplash, leaves states building their own programs.
revenue_model: $3-8K fixed admin fee per acquisition, and later a bridge-loan spread.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not money but cash timing and paperwork, and governments will pay for throughput more readily than for software.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with repetitive-loss acquisition backlogs and offer to run 20 properties under a $25K pilot. Publish time-to-close as the benchmark.

title: Displaced Insurance Agents Become Rooftop Solar Navigators
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & grid x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: Recruit the micro-agents wiped out by India's proposed insurance commission cuts as the trust-and-paperwork channel for rooftop solar, batteries and induction retrofits, paid per install by installers and lenders.
customer: MNRE-empanelled EPC installers and lenders (PSU banks, NBFCs) who pay per verified install or disbursed loan. The micro-agents (POSPs, motor-insurance agents, CSC operators) are the supply side.
problem: IRDAI's 2026-09-23 draft cuts general-insurance commission caps from 30% to 20%, sets 0% on motor third-party and 5% on own-damage, and PB Fintech fell 36% in one day. Hundreds of thousands of small agents in tier-2 and tier-3 towns lose most of their income. Meanwhile household solar and electrification demand is throttled by last-mile trust and paperwork (DISCOM feasibility, net-metering, subsidy claims, loans) rather than by hardware cost.
solution: A navigator app with training and payout rails. The agent walks a household through eligibility, vendor selection, DISCOM application, subsidy claim, bank loan and insurance for the new asset, earning per completed milestone. The annual motor-renewal touchpoint becomes the sales moment, and battery and induction bundles are added. The platform handles KYC, lead routing, quality control and payouts.
why_now: The IRDAI draft is days old and distributors such as PolicyBazaar and Turtlemint are squeezed and looking for new products. India's government-backed rooftop programs (verify current PM Surya Ghar terms) and LPG-shock induction demand are pulling households toward electrification, and UPI makes micro-payouts cheap.
revenue_model: INR 3,000-6,000 per installed home from the EPC (about 2-4% of net system cost), INR 1,000-2,000 per loan from lenders, insurance attach for the new asset, with the platform keeping 20-30% of bounties.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation just stranded a trusted, KYC'd, paperwork-fluent field force at the exact moment the bottleneck in electrification moved from hardware cost to last-mile trust. Insurance micro-agents are a distribution network searching for a product, and rooftop solar is a product searching for distribution.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 agents in one district through motor-insurance agent WhatsApp and Telegram communities and CSC networks. Sign 2 local EPCs on a per-commissioned-install bounty, run 20 installs end to end, and measure conversion from renewal touchpoints. Pay agents by UPI after commissioning.

title: Insured Filing Clerk for Multi-City Contractor Licenses
one_liner: A computer-use agent that renews and files contractor and business licenses across city and county portals that have no APIs, backed by a penalty warranty.
customer: Trade contractors (electricians, plumbers, HVAC, roofers, landscapers, painters), mobile groomers, food trucks and short-term-rental hosts working across many cities or counties, with 2-30 employees.
problem: Each city and county has its own business-license, registration and permit portal, fee schedule and renewal date, with COI and bond uploads. Missing one triggers fines or stop-work orders. Enterprise-priced compliance vendors ignore small firms, and payroll vendors are bundling only payroll compliance (Gusto bought Mosey in April 2026).
solution: An agent operates the same portals a human would to renew, upload COIs and bonds, pay fees with a virtual card and capture receipts. Human reviewers verify sensitive steps. A warranty pays penalties for missed or incorrect filings. Every filing improves a jurisdiction knowledge base of forms, fees and quirks.
why_now: Browser and computer-use agents crossed a reliability threshold in 2025-26, and payroll compliance has been productized, leaving licenses and permits as the untouched adjacent layer.
revenue_model: $59/month plus $15 per filing plus fee pass-through, with the warranty cost built into pricing.
non_obvious_insight: With roughly 19,000 municipalities, no API strategy will ever cover the map, but an agent that uses the human interface can. The moat is the jurisdiction graph and the warranty.
first_30_days: Pick a dense metro cluster with many cities and one trade. Assist 20 contractors with renewals, recording each portal flow, and sign a COI and bond partner for bulk uploads. Track error rate and hours saved.

title: Wet-Lab Materials Bill-of-Materials Scanner
one_liner: Black Duck for biology: scan a startup's plasmids, cell lines, antibodies and enzymes for license, MTA and patent encumbrances before an investor or acquirer does.
customer: Venture-backed biotechs 6-12 months from a Series B, IPO or M&A, acquirers' diligence teams, university spinouts, and IP counsel.
problem: Materials used freely in academia carry limits in for-profit use: Addgene third-party limited-use label licenses, research-only cell-line licenses, Cas9, base-editor and promoter patents, and MTA restrictions. Nobody inventories a lab's biological dependencies, so surprises surface in diligence and cut price or delay closing. At least 12 funded biotechs were sold for $1B+ in 2026, so acquirer diligence is intense.
solution: Ingest LIMS or Benchling exports, plasmid GenBank files and strain and cell-line lists. Match them against a curated encumbrance database (Addgene label-license data, depositor MTAs, patent sequence claims, vendor terms). Output a risk-ranked report with remediation options (license, replace, design around), continuous scanning as inventory changes, and attorney-reviewed summaries.
why_now: Deal volume is high, LIMS exports are easy, and software license scanning is a well-understood category that buyers already recognize.
revenue_model: $12-40k per scan, $30-100k annual continuous monitoring, and sprint pricing for acquirers' diligence teams.
non_obvious_insight: In software, license scanning is standard. In biology the dependencies are physical, unlisted and cross borders, so no bill of materials exists. One database sells to both sides: acquirers use it to find hidden liabilities, startups use it to fix them cheaply before the deal.
first_30_days: Build scanner v0 for plasmid sequences against about 200 known encumbered parts and labels. Run free scans for 10 startups through the SynBioBeta network and convert 3 to $12-15k audits. Recruit an IP attorney as advisor.

title: Immunogenicity Screens for De Novo Proteins
one_liner: A fast, low-cost HLA-diverse T-cell screen and de-immunize-and-retest loop built for AI-designed proteins that have no natural template to humanize.
customer: AI protein-design startups and pharma teams with de novo miniprotein or binder programs approaching IND, and design-tool vendors who want immunogenicity data as proof of quality.
problem: Trend chain: AI binder design is cheap and abundant. Designs are entering the clinic (a de novo PD-L1 miniprotein has reached first-in-human imaging). But de novo proteins have no germline or humanization playbook, in silico epitope predictors over-call risk, and ex vivo T-cell panels are custom studies at CROs. PBMC vials cost about $460 each, so early-stage designers skip the test until a late failure.
solution: Bulk-buy an HLA-typed donor PBMC bank (30-50 donors covering major alleles). Run 96-well T-cell activation and proliferation assays plus MHC-associated peptide analysis on batches of 20-100 candidates per week. Return per-sequence hotspot maps, feed AI deimmunization redesign, then retest. Publish calibration against known immunogenic and non-immunogenic clinical proteins.
why_now: AI-drug funding tops $6B in 2026, and frontier-lab designs hit about 27% in Adaptyv's blind test, so many de novo programs are heading toward IND. FDA's shift toward human-relevant in vitro methods favors ex vivo immunogenicity assays.
revenue_model: $2-5k per candidate at batch scale, $50-150k for full deimmunization campaigns, and platform subscriptions for design companies.
non_obvious_insight: The cost driver is donors, not reagents. Buying donor lots at scale and running big plate batches flips the economics from 'per-molecule custom study' to 'per plate'. Every screen also calibrates the predictors that AI designers will later pay for, which builds a data flywheel.
first_30_days: Contract an existing immunology lab staffed by ex-CRO scientists. Order 30 HLA-typed PBMC lots at bulk pricing. Test 10 published de novo binders and 5 clinical reference proteins. Publish a preprint and pitch 10 protein-design startups.

title: Safety Compliance-as-a-Service for Robot Deployments
one_liner: A standing team plus software that produces the risk assessments, safety validation and insurer paperwork every facility needs before deploying AMRs, cobots or humanoid pilots.
customer: EHS and operations directors at mid-size 3PLs, manufacturers and food or cold-storage plants, integrators without in-house safety staff, and insurers who want documentation.
problem: Deployments stall at safety sign-off. ISO 10218 was revised in 2025, standards for dynamically stable robots and humanoids are still being written, integrators are overloaded, and insurers and OSHA ask for documented assessments. Amazon's 1M-robot scale keeps injury scrutiny high.
solution: Field engineers plus templated software: site scan, risk assessment against current standards, laser-scanner zone and e-stop validation, speed-and-separation testing, training records and incident logs, with annual recertification. Offer a premium 'humanoid pilot safety case' product.
why_now: Humanoid pilots are moving into real facilities in 2026 (Figure reports about 350 units delivered, Agility has a $300M+ single-customer order) while standards lag. Insurers are starting to require paperwork, so it is a channel as well as a service.
revenue_model: $8-25k per site assessment, $3-8k a year for recertification, and software seats for integrators.
non_obvious_insight: For many humanoid and AMR pilots the true bottleneck is one safety officer's signature, and almost no independent practitioners exist. Insurers will steer clients to whoever produces accepted documentation, which gives you distribution.
first_30_days: Recruit a certified functional-safety engineer as cofounder and build assessment templates. Sell 3 fixed-price assessments at about $10k each from integrators' backlogs, and publish a free humanoid pilot safety checklist to generate inbound.

title: Human Concierge for Phone-Free Adults
one_liner: A $29 per month phone number staffed by humans who handle the app-only chores of modern life (QR menus, parking, rides, boarding passes, 2FA migration) so people can keep their dumbphone.
customer: Adults 25-55 who switched to flip phones, a Light Phone or a stripped-down iPhone, or want to but keep failing; first found in dumbphone communities and among buyers of minimalist phone brands, then tech workers and parents who go phone-free alongside their teens.
problem: People do not abandon dumbphones from lack of willpower but from friction: authenticator-only two-factor logins, QR-code menus, parking and transit apps, rideshare, mobile boarding passes and app-only bank features. Then they buy the smartphone back. Device makers respond by adding features (cameras, maps, apps), which recreates the problem. As the flip-phone revival hits the mainstream in 2026, the failure rate is the business opportunity.
solution: Two products. First, a one-time 'Switch Day' ($99): a human sits with the customer for two hours, ports the number, migrates 2FA away from authenticator apps to hardware keys, voice codes or email, moves bank alerts to text and voice, prints backup codes and paper maps. Second, 'the Desk', a call/text line staffed by humans with a company smartphone and virtual cards: they book the ride to your address, pay the parking zone by plate, read you the QR menu, print or hand over the boarding pass, and make the reservation that only exists in an app. Fair-use unlimited requests on the subscription, with pay-per-errand for heavier tasks.
why_now: The dumbphone and analog movement hit mainstream press in 2026 (Fortune's Gen Z analog coverage in February, new flip-phone startups launching in September), while schools in about 40 states now restrict phones, pushing parents to model the behavior. Meanwhile, essential services keep going app-only. Cheap voice and workflow tools let a small human team serve dozens of subscribers per agent.
revenue_model: $29 per month subscription, $99 Switch Day setup fee, bundle and referral deals with dumbphone makers (a Desk membership included with each device), employer perk for 'focus' or wellness programs, and per-errand fees for premium requests.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce product in the anti-screen economy is not another device but human proxies for the smartphone-shaped holes in society. The business grows every time a restaurant or city makes something QR-only, and every new mandate is a marketing lead. Abstainers are also a tight, vocal community, so each retained customer is an ambassador, and the manufacturers gain from a service that reduces returns.
first_30_days: Offer 20 people in dumbphone communities a free Switch Day in exchange for interviews and permission to log every request. Run the Desk by hand from one shared iPhone, a Google Voice number and an Airtable. Categorize the first 300 requests to find the top 10 that drive 80% of the pain. Convert users to $29 per month and approach two minimalist phone brands about bundling. Target 100 paying members by month 5.

title: Compliant Format Kit for Card-Break Sellers
one_liner: Counsel-designed formats and software that let breakers, repackers and game stores run randomized break and mystery-pack sales without tripping lottery law.
customer: Independent breakers and repack sellers on Whatnot, eBay and TikTok, plus game stores that run break nights.
problem: Random spot-assignment breaks are being attacked as illegal lotteries under California Penal Code 319. Fifteen arbitration demands were filed in March 2026 for 30+ clients (about 100 expected). A July 2025 suit names Whatnot and Fanatics Live, and a qui tam action was recently unsealed. Independent sellers carry exposure with no counsel and no tooling.
solution: Alternative formats (pick-your-own-team, guaranteed-value floors, no-purchase-necessary entry flows), a per-state rule engine with registration and bonding reminders, an audit-logged randomizer with retained video, age and spend-limit controls, odds-disclosure templates, and dispute-ready records.
why_now: Arbitrations run 12-18 months, so seller uncertainty peaks through 2027. Platforms are defending, not building seller tooling.
revenue_model: $79-299/month SaaS by seller volume, a legal-review add-on, compliance audits, and licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation targets platforms, but the marginal legal risk sits with small sellers whose margins cannot absorb it. Nobody sells them a compliant product design, and the fix is to change the product (make assignment non-random or value-guaranteed), which software can standardize. Whether breaks are illegal is unsettled, so retain gaming counsel.
first_30_days: Retain consumer-gaming counsel. Publish a free state-by-state cheat sheet. Recruit 20 mid-size breakers through Discords and pilot a pick-your-spot format with a guaranteed floor at $99/month.
